sq.q: Explain how a stack can be used to reverse a list. Write the algorithm and briefly justify why a stack is suitable for this task.
answer: A stack is a linear data structure that allows insertion and deletion of elements only from one end, called the top of the stack. It follows the Last-In, First-Out (LIFO) principle, meaning the last element added is the first one to be removed.

This LIFO nature makes the stack highly suitable for reversing a list. When we push each element of a list onto the stack, the element at the beginning of the list becomes the bottom of the stack and the last element becomes the top. When we pop the elements back into the list, the order of elements gets reversed automatically.
To reverse a list using a stack:
Traverse the original list and push all elements into the stack.
Pop elements one by one from the stack and overwrite them back into the list.

// Step 2: Pop elements from stack and overwrite the list

LIFO Nature: When elements are popped, they come out in the reverse order of how they were pushed. This property is perfect for reversing sequences .

sq.q: Describe the process of checking balanced symbols using a stack. What types of symbols are usually considered, and what will the stack contain during the process?
answer: In programming languages and expressions, symbols like (), {}, and [] are often used to group expressions or statements. To ensure that every opening symbol has a corresponding closing symbol, we use a technique called balanced symbol checking. A stack is the ideal data structure for this task because of its Last-In, First-Out (LIFO) behavior.
Process of Checking Balanced Symbols Using a Stack:
Scan the expression from left to right, one character at a time.
For every opening symbol ((, {, [): Push it onto the stack.

For every closing symbol (), }, ]): Check if the stack is empty. If it is, the expression is unbalanced (no corresponding opening symbol). Otherwise, pop the top element from the stack. Check if the popped opening symbol matches the current closing symbol. If it doesn't match, the expression is unbalanced .

lq.q: You are developing a calculator app for a mobile device that evaluates arithmetic expressions entered by users. Since mobile processors are optimized for postfix (Reverse Polish Notation) evaluation, you must first convert the user-entered infix expressions into postfix form. One such user input is the infix expression: K + L - M * N + (O ^ P) * W / U / V * T + Q Based on this scenario: Write the algorithm for converting an infix expression to a postfix expression using a stack. Apply your algorithm step-by-step to convert the given expression into its postfix form .
answer: 1. Initialize an empty stack for operators and an empty list for output.
2. Scan the infix expression from left to right.
a. If it is an operand (e.g., A-Z), add it directly to the output.
b. If it is an opening parenthesis ‘(’, push it onto the stack.
c. If it is a closing parenthesis ‘)’, pop from the stack and add to the output until an opening parenthesis is encountered. Pop and discard the '('.
d. If it is an operator (e.g., +, -, *, /, ^):
If the incoming symbol has higher precedence than the top of the stack, push it on the stack.
If the incoming symbol has lower precedence than the top of the stack, pop and print the top of the stack. Then test the incoming operator against the new top of the stack.

If the incoming operator has the same precedence with the top of the stack then use the associativity rules. If the associativity is from left to right then pop and print the top of the stack then push the incoming operator. If the associativity is from right to left then push the incoming operator.
4. After scanning the expression, pop all remaining operators from the stack and add to output.
